items.name: 递进
items.plain: 有几对相邻章节，后一章的开头把前一章刚做完的事重新描述了一遍，没有带来新东西；另外全片主角性别前后不一，导致第六章靠性别规则推动的关键情节成立与否取决于你选哪个答案。

problems.text: CH04 和 CH05 的目的写得很像(相似度 0.5)
CH06 和 CH07 的目的写得很像(相似度 0.45)
CH12 和 CH13 的目的写得很像(相似度 0.45)
（程序确定）CH04 以「大家等着抛球」结束，CH05 的目的描述开头仍在描述「你在底层区域挤着」，把同一个底层社交场景铺了两遍才进入抛球本身。
problems.fix: 把 CH05 的 purpose 改成直接从「球飞下来的一刻」开头，不再重述你在底层挤着的处境。

problems.text: （程序确定）CH06 以「站到场边」结束，CH07 的 purpose 开头再次描述「你沿着邻座给的路线下来，手里攥着球，站在元老席边缘当闯入者」，重述了 CH06 刚完成的到达过程。
problems.fix: 删去 CH07 purpose 里关于「沿路线下来」和「到达场边」的描述，直接从观察元老席与沙地开始。

problems.text: （程序确定）CH12 以「热闹背后的代价」作过渡，CH13 的 purpose 开头「The water show is only part of the answer」仍在回扣水上场面，然后才进入代价；两章交接处重叠了对「场面本身」的定性。
problems.fix: 把 CH13 的 purpose 改成直接从「水上表演结束后你看到的」开始，不再用「水上表演只是答案的一部分」来重新引入上一章。

problems.text: （请判断）主角设定写「平民男子」，但问题链、开场合同、CH06 的情节全用「女子」身份——CH06 靠「女性不得进入元老席区域」驱动整个限时潜入，若主角改回男性，这一章的阻碍机制需要完全换掉。
problems.fix: 在蓝图顶层的主角设定字段统一写「外来女子」，并删去「平民男子」的表述，三章不用另改（蓝图已按女子写）。

items.name: 事实支撑
items.plain: 有一个单元靠还没确认的制作信息才能写，以及一条事实被标成「回顾」但它在蓝图里根本还没出现过——这两处如果不改，写稿时会卡住。

problems.text: CH01 的 B5-B7 单元（30字，制作方法说明）的唯一依据是 F34，而 F34 标注「须由制作方确认」，画面来源、工具、工作量全部未知；这个单元无法在制作方确认前写出任何具体内容。
problems.fix: 在 CH01 的 B5-B7 单元备注「内容待制作方确认后填入」，并将对应字数（30字）暂列为弹性预算，避免写稿时用占位内容凑字。

problems.text: F11（马提亚尔表演诗成书年代存疑）出现在 CH10 的 recap_ids 里，意味着它应当在 CH10 之前已经用过；但检查全部前置章节，没有任何章节的 fact_ids 或 recap_ids 收录过 F11，它实际上到 CH12 才第一次作为 fact_id 出现，CH10 不可能回顾一条尚未引入的事实。
problems.fix: 将 F11 从 CH10 的 recap_ids 移入 CH10 的 fact_ids，并将 CH12 的 fact_ids 中的 F11 改入 recap_ids，使引入顺序与章节顺序一致。

notes.text: 蓝图自查(中等):人称有冲突：节拍表和选定钩子用「I」，问题链是代入式「你」。蓝图开头按节拍表保留「I」，第二章起的目标按「你」写；写稿前应定一种口径，避免两种语体混用。。请判断是不是真问题
蓝图自查(中等):画面素材、复原方法和工作量（F34）仍待查，第5拍和第7拍须制作方确认后才能照说。。请判断是不是真问题

写前分析的反转验证:事实 F08、F11、F14 和反转结论相反(没有查到能推翻「史家写下场内注水」的材料，考古公园官网反而支持开幕海战。反方有三点：苏维托尼乌斯把提图斯的海战记在旧海战池；马提亚尔表演诗的年代和场合有疑问；供水线路缺少考古证据，且狄奥说的「突然」与现代推算的半小时到数小时注水时间不好对上。这三点放在 FS12 正面讲。另外，原分析所说「开幕时地下层很可能还没建成」只是一种意见，官网称当时有木结构地下层（F02）。)

rounds.summary: 蓝图的核心结构和证据链是完整的，反转有史料支撑、反方证据也有正面处理。需要改的问题集中在两处：三对相邻章节（CH04/05、CH06/07、CH12/13）的交接处有重述，每处只需修改后一章的 purpose 开头；主角性别在设定字段与正文之间不一致，统一写女性即可，不涉及内容重写。事实层面有两个结构性小错：一个单元靠未确认的制作信息支撑，以及一条事实被错误地列为「回顾」却从未在前面引入，各改一个字段就能解决。

angles.belief: 斗兽场是罗马文明与建造才能的象征，代表帝国的强盛与工程天才
angles.claim: 斗兽场由 Titus 征服耶路撒冷后掠夺圣殿的战利品出资兴建，主要劳动力来自犹太战争（66–73 AD）被俘的犹太奴隶——开幕日坐在观众席上欢呼的人，坐的正是用另一个民族的血与财富堆起来的台阶
angles.one_line: 你以为这是罗马人的骄傲，它其实是一座用战利品和奴隶搭成的战争纪念碑
angles.key_fact: 需查：学者 Géza Alföldy 于1990年代重新解读斗兽场外墙铭文残迹，认为原文含 'ex manubiis'（战利品所得）字样，结合文献指向犹太战争战利品；Josephus《犹太战争》记载提图斯将数万犹太俘虏送往罗马充当劳役
angles.why_watch: 开幕日欢呼最响的那一刻，藏着观众从未听说过的另一段历史——走进去才能感受到这层重量
angles.risk: 铭文解读有争议，部分学者认为'ex manubiis'指向不够确定；劳动力构成的考古证据不充分，不能说'全部是犹太奴隶'，措辞需留余地

angles.belief: 斗兽场从第一天起就是陆上角斗的场地，这是它唯一的用途
angles.claim: Cassius Dio 和 Suetonius 均记载 Titus 开幕庆典包含模拟海战（naumachia）——斗兽场在开幕最初几天可能真的被注满了水；但学界至今争论这究竟发生在场内还是附近水域，争议点正是地下层（hypogeum）80 AD 时是否已完工
angles.one_line: 你以为开幕日是角斗士登场，史书说第一幕可能是水战——这栋建筑从第一天起就比你想象的更奇怪
angles.key_fact: 需查：Cassius Dio《罗马史》66.25 对提图斯开幕庆典 naumachia 的原文描述；现代考古研究对 hypogeum 完工年代（Domitian 时期才完成？）的结论
angles.why_watch: 主角穿越落地后发现场地里全是水，会是全片最大的意外落地时刻，把观众对斗兽场的全部前置认知直接推翻
angles.risk: 多数现代学者倾向于认为 naumachia 在斗兽场外的 Stagnum Neronis 举行，若此论点查明为'场外'则需降格为'开幕庆典的一部分而非场内奇观'

angles.belief: 斗兽场 80 AD 的开幕是罗马帝国最鼎盛时刻的庆典，整座城市都在狂欢
angles.claim: 开幕庆典的一百天里，罗马城同时遭遇史上破坏最惨的一场大火（连续烧三天，吞噬神庙与图书馆），而就在前一年维苏威刚埋掉了 Pompeii，之后瘟疫接踵而至；Titus 本人在庆典结束约一年后驾崩，年仅四十出头——这场"盛典"的背景幕布是连环灾难
angles.one_line: 你以为这是帝国的顶点，其实站在开幕日的斗兽场里，四面都是正在燃烧的罗马
angles.key_fact: 需查：Suetonius《提图斯传》第八节关于火灾（'incendium…per triduum'，持续三天）与瘟疫的记载；Cassius Dio 确认大火发生在庆典进行期间（80 AD）；Titus 卒于 81 AD 9月，距开幕庆典约一年
angles.why_watch: 框架的倒计时结构天然契合：主角站在庆典人群里欢呼，身后是正在燃烧的天空——'繁荣'与'崩解'同框，戏剧反讽密度最高
angles.risk: 三个灾难叠加可能显得刻意堆砌；需确认大火确在庆典进行期间（而非庆典结束后）发生，否则同框效果减弱

checks.note: Cassius Dio 明确记载竞技场被注满水并举行水上表演（R6、R10直接引原文），2024年多篇文章（The Independent R10、Science Friday R23）均确认至少一场 naumachia 在场内举行。削弱点：R22显示地下层（hypogeum）在Domitian时期约80-82年完工，意味着开幕时地下层尚未竣工或刚开工，arena地板尚为实地可密封——这反而在技术上支持注水可能；但R25引述历史学家认为防水工程难度极高普遍存疑。两方证据并存，属于真实学界争议，M3结构可以直接用这个争议本身。
checks.narrowed: 古代史书（Cassius Dio）明确记载斗兽场在开幕庆典期间被注满水；现代考古学者仍在争论，但2024年最新研究倾向于认为至少一场 naumachia 确实发生在场内——'你以为它从第一天起就是陆战竞技场'这个前提可以被拆掉，争议本身就是故事。

pick.why: A1 有最硬的物证基础：Alföldy 对铭文的重建经过 Brill 学术出版、Biblical Archaeology Society 等多条独立来源交叉印证，'战利品出资'这个核心事实有刻在石头上的东西撑着，不是推断。A2 的水战角度很抓眼球，但核心张力是'考古界还在争'，视频必须靠一个尚未定论的问题带观众走，风险更高；A3 的'同框燃烧'最强的说法（庆典进行期间大火同步）被R12削弱，降格为'同年'之后反差力减弱，且需要补查的关键时序事实尚未到手。A1 的道德反差最能接住框架的核心情绪——第一人称站在台阶上欢呼时忽然意识到这块石头的来历，正是'读过与活过是两种完全不同的知道'那句话的最有力的载体；M3 能精准拆掉'罗马文明象征'这个几乎人人都持有的前提，M8 的外推也自然（'你还会进哪座用征服建起的建筑'）。

final.belief: 斗兽场从开幕第一天起就是陆上角斗的场地，这是它唯一的用途
final.claim: 公元80年开幕庆典期间，斗兽场曾被注满水举行模拟海战——Cassius Dio 留下了文字记录，2024年考古研究也倾向认为这至少发生过一次；你脑子里'角斗士对决'的第一印象，连开场都拿错了
final.one_line: 你以为开幕第一幕是角斗士，史书记下来的却是皇帝命人把整个竞技场注满了水
final.ending_landing: 一栋你以为彻底了解的建筑，连第一天的用法都和你想的不一样——你还有几个'当然知道'其实根本没查过？
final.boundary: 仅适用于开幕庆典期间的具体场景；不适用于断言斗兽场'常规'举行水战（后期地下层建成后无法注水）

facts.content: Géza Alföldy 约1995年发现斗兽场外墙铭文背后的金属字母孔洞，经重建认定原铭文含'ex manubiis'（战利品所得）字样，孔洞年代追溯至公元79-80年，铭文记录建筑由Vespasian下令、以征服犹太人的战利品出资兴建
facts.year: 约79-80 AD（铭文年代）；1995年左右（Alföldy重建）
facts.note: 铭文系重建而非完整留存；R35中Alfoldy结论被Feldman进一步推断指向犹太大起义，但两人结论互补而非同一人

thesis_card.viewer_belief: 斗兽场就是一片沙地，开幕庆典上演的就是角斗士厮杀
thesis_card.truth: 卡西乌斯·狄奥写下，提图斯在开幕庆典中突然把这座剧场注满水，放进受过训练的动物，还让人乘船打了一场海战。斗兽场考古公园官网也认可开幕海战，但它是否发生、怎样做到，学界仍有争论
thesis_card.one_line_thesis: 你以为斗兽场开幕就是沙地上的角斗，可一位罗马史家写下的是：皇帝把整座场地灌满了水。
thesis_card.ending_landing: 下次你在照片或电影里看见斗兽场的沙地，你会想起有人写过它装满水的样子：认得一栋建筑和查过它，是两回事。
thesis_card.differs_from_source_conclusion: 相同点是落在两种「知道」的差别上。原片比的是读过和活过，落点是哀伤；本片比的是以为知道和查过记载，落点是认知翻转，哀伤只由动物屠杀和提图斯的结局承担。注水论点由本题自己的狄奥、马提亚尔文本和考古公园说法支撑
thesis_card.contrast: 翻案：从干燥的角斗沙场翻到注水的海战场地
thesis_card.double_standard: 同在一座建筑里看同一场演出，元老坐在最靠近场地的位置，穿深色斗篷的平民和女性只能往高处去
thesis_card.boundary: 这里说的只是开幕庆典中的记载，它是否发生、场地下面当时什么样，至今有争论。

facts.content: 卡西乌斯·狄奥记载提图斯在开幕庆典中把这座剧场注满水，带入马、牛等受过训练、能在水中活动的动物，又让人乘船打海战
开幕时场地下面是什么样，说法不一。斗兽场考古公园官网称：地下层在开幕时为木结构，图密善时期改为砖石结构；通向两端的通道曾在开幕海战中当船坞用。另有资料认为地下层是图密善时期才建的。现在看到的砖石地下迷宫不是公元80年的样子
facts.source: Parco archeologico del Colosseo 官网；Encyclopaedia Romana

facts.content: 开幕庆典持续一百天。狄奥记约九千只驯养和野生动物被杀（他把剧场与浴场的落成庆典合在一起叙述），一些身份不高的女性参与了宰杀
狄奥《罗马史》66.25：提图斯突然把这座剧场注满水，带入马、牛和受训在水中活动的家畜；又有人乘船扮作科基拉人与科林斯人打海战。狄奥晚于事件一个多世纪写作
狄奥没有说剧场注水是哪一天。他所记「第一天角斗和猎兽、第三天海战」是城外盖乌斯与卢基乌斯林苑一带的场次，那里第一天是在湖面铺木板后举行的
提图斯从高处向剧场里抛刻字小木球，接到的人可兑换食物、衣服、金银器皿、马匹、牲口乃至奴隶
狄奥记有鹤相斗、四头象相斗；剧场与浴场落成庆典中约九千只驯养和野生动物被杀，一些身份不高的女性参与宰杀
苏维托尼乌斯把提图斯的模拟海战记在旧海战池，并写到一天之内展示五千只野兽
苏维托尼乌斯记图密善也在圆形剧场里办过海战，因此不能说水战只在开幕时有过
facts.source: Suetonius, Domitian 4（经 Encyclopaedia Romana 引述）

facts.content: 马提亚尔第24首对远道而来的迟到观众说：眼前的水和船别让你误会，这里刚才还是陆地
马提亚尔这组表演诗的成书年代和所指场合有不确定处，有译本题名归到图密善时期
facts.source: Pomona 学院资料页（1897年匿名译本）; Heurist 数据库说明

facts.content: 工程师 Martin Crapper 2007年研究认为注水可行：地下部分有灰浆抹面，水可能来自 Claudia 水道的一条支线。场内有供饮水和排水的管渠，但没有考古证据证明供水线路怎样接进场地、水量怎样控制，供水方案仍是推测
现代推算从约半小时到约三个半小时不等：Crapper 估34至76分钟（用的场地尺寸偏小，后来发过更正）；按另一种场地尺寸和流量约83分钟；考虑水道实际损耗约3.5小时。稿中只说「从半小时左右到几个小时」
有考古学者因缺少管道证据和场地偏小而怀疑；Heinz-Jürgen Beste 认为可能用了专门造的小船。地下层建成后水战难以再办
K. M. Coleman《Launching into History: Aquatic Displays in the Early Empire》，Journal of Roman Studies 83 (1993): 48-74。摘要页可见的一条脚注指出：竞技场地板架在地下墙体上的看法已被普遍接受，而文献所记的场内海战仍需要解释。正文结论未读到
facts.source: Cambridge Core 摘要页；University of Mannheim 书目

facts.content: 苏维托尼乌斯记奥古斯都时期规定：公共演出首排留给元老，穿深色斗篷者不得坐中部，女性看角斗只能在高处。套用到80年的斗兽场属于推定。斗兽场考古公园官网也说最靠近场地的座位保留给元老
facts.source: Suetonius, Augustus 44（BCcampus 史料集）；Parco archeologico del Colosseo 官网
facts.year: 奥古斯都时期规定；斗兽场座次为后人研究

facts.content: 看台分为前排台座和其上数层，最高处是木结构廊座，穷人和女性在上面。该木廊在80年是否已完工待查
通行说法是观众凭座位凭证入场，上面标分区、排和座号；80年当时的实物凭证待查
各阶层观众从76个编号拱门入场，编号刻出并涂红，北侧现仍可见29个
facts.source: Parco archeologico del Colosseo 官网

facts.content: 阿尔瓦尔祭司团公元80年的石刻记录写明了他们在这座剧场分到的座位空间，现代解读约合37米长
facts.source: the-colosseum.net ; Biblical Archaeology Society 注释（CIL VI 铭文，ILS 5049）

facts.content: 斗兽场入场免费，座位按社会身份划分
facts.source: Parco archeologico del Colosseo 官网；Smithsonian Magazine

facts.content: 常见估计约容纳五万人，也有更高的估计
竞技场地面为木板铺沙，下方有地下空间；开幕时下面的构造有分歧（见 F02）
facts.source: Turismo Roma；Parco archeologico del Colosseo 官网

facts.content: 剧场有帆布遮阳篷，由水手操作。80年开幕时的使用情况待查
2022年公布的排水道清理发现无花果、葡萄、橄榄、坚果遗存和熊与大型猫科骨头。这些反映的是剧场长期使用情况，不能定到80年
马提亚尔第29首写角斗士普里斯库斯与维鲁斯势均力敌，皇帝让两人同时获得解除比斗的木剑
庆典结束时，提图斯当着民众痛哭。原因史料没有定论
提图斯于公元81年9月13日去世，时年41岁（苏维托尼乌斯说他在第42个年头），死在其父去世的同一处农庄
开幕年份通行说法为公元80年（个别写80-81）。确切月日没有可靠记载；网上偶见的6月29日、4月等说法没有查到原始依据，不可上稿
马提亚尔第3首写色雷斯、萨尔马提亚、阿拉伯、埃塞俄比亚等远方的人都来到罗马观看
2024年电影《Gladiator II》呈现了斗兽场水战并加入鲨鱼
邻座向导、潜入前排的路线与时间窗、与提图斯随从的对话、主角穿越身份均为虚构，稿中第一次出现时统一交代
若九千只动物平均分到一百天，每天约九十只。实际分布未知，九千这个数还可能包含浴场落成的场次，苏维托尼乌斯另有单日五千只的说法。仅供内部理解，稿中不使用日均数
facts.method: 9000只 ÷ 100天 = 90只/天（假设平均分布，史料不支持这个假设）

facts.content: 须由制作方确认。钩子节拍里的现行草稿是「依据罗马文字记载和现存遗址做照片级复原」，尚未证实；画面实际用了什么素材、什么工具、工作量多大都不知道
考古学家认为斗兽场设有饮水泉和厕所；数量、位置以及公元80年开幕时是否启用不明
Alföldy 1995年依据钉孔复原的铭文，大意是皇帝提图斯下令用战利品建造这座新的圆形剧场（原为韦斯帕芗而作，后加入提图斯名号）。这是复原而非现存文字，2026年仍有研究团队用激光扫描重新检讨（本片未选此角度）
facts.source: CIL VI 40454a 说明页（Judaism and Rome）；匈牙利科学院机构库；AIAC 讲座摘要

facts.content: 据我所知没有古代文献给出犹太战俘在建造劳动力中的比例，流传的「三万人」一类数字缺少原始依据，不确定（本片未选此角度，不上稿）
据我所知没有史料明确记载犹太战俘在80年开幕庆典中上场；是否有奴隶或死刑犯以何种身份出场，需另核马提亚尔表演诗（本片不上稿）
我认为最相关的是《犹太战争》6.418前后：部分成年战俘被送往埃及服苦役，另一些分送各行省死于竞技场。我不知道有哪一段明确说战俘被送到罗马修建斗兽场，不确定（本片不上稿）
据我所知没有史料能逐阶段区分战利品资金和提图斯续资，不确定（本片不上稿）
斗兽场考古公园官网把开幕庆典的场内海战写作史实，并称地下两端的通道当时用作船坞；改成砖石地下结构后不再办水上表演。页面摘要未见所列证据，学界仍有争议
facts.source: Parco archeologico del Colosseo 官网

thesis_check.note: 没有查到能推翻「史家写下场内注水」的材料，考古公园官网反而支持开幕海战。反方有三点：苏维托尼乌斯把提图斯的海战记在旧海战池；马提亚尔表演诗的年代和场合有疑问；供水线路缺少考古证据，且狄奥说的「突然」与现代推算的半小时到数小时注水时间不好对上。这三点放在 FS12 正面讲。另外，原分析所说「开幕时地下层很可能还没建成」只是一种意见，官网称当时有木结构地下层（F02）。

opening_beats.new_line: Enjoy, guys. This was a lot of work.

opening_beats.new_line: Just between you and me, I want to get as close as I can: the senators' seats, the emperor's box, the sand itself.

opening_beats.src_line: I also want to try to talk to the captain about the iceberg. I feel like someone should at least try to say something.

opening_beats.src_line: Wish me luck.
opening_beats.new_line: Wish me luck.

"facts": [
{"id": "F01", "slot": "核心记载", "content": "卡西乌斯·狄奥记载提图斯开幕庆典期间竞技场被注满水，马、牛等动物在水中表演，人乘船参与水上表演", "kind": "事实", "source": "Internet Archive ; The Independent", "url": "https://archive.org/download/devitacaesaruml00pricgoog/devitacaesaruml00pricgoog_text.pdf#12#19#12 ; https://www.the-independent.com/arts-entertainment/films/news/gladiator-2-colosseum-sharks-water-battles-true-story-b2652717.html#1", "year": "80", "region": "罗马", "freshness": "不适用", "method": ""},
{"id": "F02", "slot": "地下结构", "content": "地下层在约公元80至82年作为第二期工程建成，原设计没有它。开幕时地板下的确切状态，来源没有说明", "kind": "事实", "source": "Colosseo Roma - Guida Informativa", "url": "https://colosseum.roma.it/en/underground/#what-to-see-underground", "year": "约80-82", "region": "罗马", "freshness": "不适用", "method": ""},
{"id": "F03", "slot": "庆典规模", "content": "开幕庆典历时一百多天，约九千只动物被杀，女性也参与了竞技场表演", "kind": "事实", "source": "Internet Archive ; The Independent ; Wikimedia", "url": "https://archive.org/download/devitacaesaruml00pricgoog/devitacaesaruml00pricgoog_text.pdf#12#19#12 ; https://www.the-independent.com/arts-entertainment/films/news/gladiator-2-colosseum-sharks-water-battles-true-story-b2652717.html#1 ; https://lists.wikimedia.org/hyperkitty/list/daily-article-l@lists.wikimedia.org/message/XEB5YCI7C45ZXTWSMS5AQZTIFKS47VOX/", "year": "80", "region": "罗马", "freshness": "不适用", "method": ""},
{"id": "F04", "slot": "原始文献", "content": "狄奥《罗马史》66.25：提图斯突然把这座剧场注满水，带入马、牛和受训在水中活动的家畜；又有人乘船扮作科基拉人与科林斯人打海战。狄奥晚于事件一个多世纪写作", "kind": "事实", "source": "Cassius Dio, Roman History 66.25 (Loeb, LacusCurtius)", "url": "https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Cassius_Dio/66*.html", "year": "记80年事", "region": "罗马", "freshness": "不适用", "method": ""},
{"id": "F05", "slot": "顺序边界", "content": "狄奥没有说剧场注水是哪一天。他所记「第一天角斗和猎兽、第三天海战」是城外盖乌斯与卢基乌斯林苑一带的场次，那里第一天是在湖面铺木板后举行的", "kind": "事实", "source": "Cassius Dio 66.25", "url": "https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Cassius_Dio/66*.html", "year": "记80年事", "region": "罗马", "freshness": "不适用", "method": ""},
{"id": "F06", "slot": "赠品细节", "content": "提图斯从高处向剧场里抛刻字小木球，接到的人可兑换食物、衣服、金银器皿、马匹、牲口乃至奴隶", "kind": "事实", "source": "Cassius Dio 66.25", "url": "https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Cassius_Dio/66*.html", "year": "记80年事", "region": "罗马", "freshness": "不适用", "method": ""},
{"id": "F07", "slot": "节目目录", "content": "狄奥记有鹤相斗、四头象相斗，约九千只驯养和野生动物被杀，女性参与了宰杀", "kind": "事实", "source": "Cassius Dio 66.25", "url": "https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Cassius_Dio/66*.html", "year": "记80年事", "region": "罗马", "freshness": "不适用", "method": ""},
{"id": "F08", "slot": "反向记载", "content": "苏维托尼乌斯把提图斯的模拟海战记在旧海战池，并写到一天之内展示五千只野兽", "kind": "事实", "source": "Suetonius, Titus 7", "url": "https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Suetonius/12Caesars/Titus*.html", "year": "记80年事", "region": "罗马", "freshness": "不适用", "method": ""},
{"id": "F09", "slot": "后续边界", "content": "苏维托尼乌斯记图密善也在圆形剧场里办过海战，因此不能说水战只在开幕时有过", "kind": "事实", "source": "Suetonius, Domitian 4（经 Encyclopaedia Romana 引述）", "url": "https://penelope.uchicago.edu/~grout/encyclopaedia_romana/gladiators/naumachiae.html", "year": "81-96", "region": "罗马", "freshness": "不适用", "method": ""},
{"id": "F10", "slot": "同时代文字", "content": "马提亚尔第24首对远道而来的迟到观众说：眼前的水和船别让你误会，这里刚才还是陆地", "kind": "事实", "source": "Martial, De Spectaculis 24", "url": "https://www.csun.edu/~hcfll004/Martial-Colosseum.html", "year": "约80", "region": "罗马", "freshness": "不适用", "method": ""},
{"id": "F11", "slot": "文献局限", "content": "马提亚尔这组表演诗的成书年代和所指场合有不确定处，有译本题名归到图密善时期", "kind": "事实", "source": "Pomona 学院资料页（1897年匿名译本）; Heurist 数据库说明", "url": "https://pages.pomona.edu/~cmc24747/sources/martial/mart_lib_spect.htm ; https://heurist.huma-num.fr/heurist/judaism_and_rome/view/1325", "year": "不适用", "region": "罗马", "freshness": "不适用", "method": ""},
{"id": "F12", "slot": "工程研究", "content": "工程师 Martin Crapper 2007年发表研究认为注水可行，依据包括地下部分抹有灰浆、可能由水道支线供水；场内没有发现水管，供水方案仍属推测", "kind": "事实", "source": "Science Friday", "url": "https://www.sciencefriday.com/articles/gladiator-ii-the-evidence-for-colosseum-naval-battles/", "year": "2007研究", "region": "罗马", "freshness": "时效风险", "method": ""},
{"id": "F13", "slot": "注水时间", "content": "对注满场地所需时间的推算差别很大，从不到一小时到数小时都有，取决于流量和水深假设", "kind": "事实", "source": "Encyclopaedia Romana ; Science Friday", "url": "https://penelope.uchicago.edu/~grout/encyclopaedia_romana/gladiators/naumachiae.html ; https://www.sciencefriday.com/articles/gladiator-ii-the-evidence-for-colosseum-naval-battles/", "year": "现代研究", "region": "罗马", "freshness": "时效风险", "method": ""},
{"id": "F14", "slot": "学界争议", "content": "有考古学者因缺少管道证据和场地偏小而怀疑；Heinz-Jürgen Beste 认为可能用了专门造的小船。地下层建成后水战难以再办", "kind": "事实", "source": "Science Friday ; Encyclopaedia Romana", "url": "https://www.sciencefriday.com/articles/gladiator-ii-the-evidence-for-colosseum-naval-battles/ ; https://penelope.uchicago.edu/~grout/encyclopaedia_romana/gladiators/naumachiae.html", "year": "现代研究", "region": "罗马", "freshness": "近3年", "method": ""},

Coleman 1993年在 Journal of Roman Studies 讨论早期帝国水上表演，论文结论本次未读到原文", "kind": "待查", "source": "待查", "url": "https://resolve.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-roman-studies/article/abs/launching-into-history-aquatic-displays-in-the-early-empire/032C154DEB36D357E9E7D32E28F1C78F", "year": "1993", "region": "罗马", "freshness": "时效风险", "method": ""},
{"id": "F16", "slot": "座次规则", "content": "苏维托尼乌斯记奥古斯都时期规定：公共演出首排留给元老，穿深色斗篷者不得坐中部，女性看角斗只能在高处。套用到80年的斗兽场属于推定", "kind": "事实", "source": "Suetonius, Augustus 44（BCcampus 史料集）", "url": "https://pressbooks.bccampus.ca/spectaclesintheromanworldsourcebook/chapter/seating-in-the-arena-and-society/", "year": "奥古斯都时期", "region": "罗马", "freshness": "不适用", "method": ""},
{"id": "F17", "slot": "分层结构", "content": "看台分为前排台座和其上数层，最高处是木结构廊座，穷人和女性在上面。该木廊在80年是否已完工待查", "kind": "事实", "source": "the-colosseum.net", "url": "https://the-colosseum.net/wp/?p=506", "year": "复原研究", "region": "罗马", "freshness": "时效风险", "method": ""},
{"id": "F18", "slot": "入场凭证", "content": "通行说法是观众凭座位凭证入场，上面标分区、排和座号；80年当时的实物凭证待查", "kind": "事实", "source": "the-colosseum.net", "url": "https://the-colosseum.net/wp/?p=506", "year": "复原研究", "region": "罗马", "freshness": "时效风险", "method": ""},
{"id": "F19", "slot": "入口编号", "content": "底层80个拱门中76个编号供观众使用，部分编号至今可见，原先涂红", "kind": "事实", "source": "斗兽场考古公园说明牌（HMDB 收录）", "url": "https://www.hmdb.org/m.asp?m=265980", "year": "现存遗迹", "region": "罗马", "freshness": "近3年", "method": ""},
{"id": "F20", "slot": "实物铭文", "content": "阿尔瓦尔祭司团公元80年的石刻记录写明了他们在这座剧场分到的座位空间，现代解读约合37米长", "kind": "事实", "source": "the-colosseum.net ; Biblical Archaeology Society 注释（CIL VI 铭文，ILS 5049）", "url": "https://the-colosseum.net/wp/?p=506 ; https://library.biblicalarchaeology.org/?p=51293", "year": "80", "region": "罗马", "freshness": "不适用", "method": ""},
{"id": "F21", "slot": "票价身位", "content": "观看演出免费入场", "kind": "事实", "source": "Vassar College 学生考古博客（二手，建议再核）", "url": "https://pages.vassar.edu/realarchaeology/?p=4820", "year": "古罗马", "region": "罗马", "freshness": "时效风险", "method": ""},
{"id": "F22", "slot": "容量", "content": "常见估计约容纳五万人，也有更高的估计", "kind": "事实", "source": "World History Encyclopedia", "url": "https://www.worldhistory.org/Colosseum/", "year": "现代估计", "region": "罗马", "freshness": "时效风险", "method": ""},

{"id": "F24", "slot": "遮阳篷", "content": "剧场有帆布遮阳篷，由水手操作。80年开幕时的使用情况待查", "kind": "事实", "source": "World History Encyclopedia", "url": "https://www.worldhistory.org/Colosseum/Humphreys", "year": "复原研究", "region": "罗马", "freshness": "时效风险", "method": ""},
{"id": "F25", "slot": "食物遗存", "content": "2022年公布的排水道清理发现无花果、葡萄、橄榄、坚果遗存和熊与大型猫科骨头。这些反映的是剧场长期使用情况，不能定到80年", "kind": "事实", "source": "Archaeology Magazine ; RNZ", "url": "https://archaeology.org/news/2022/11/29/221130-colosseum-sewer-system ; https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/world/479467/animal-bones-ancient-romans-snack-food-found-in-colosseum", "year": "2022发现", "region": "罗马", "freshness": "时效风险", "method": ""},
{"id": "F26", "slot": "群像", "content": "马提亚尔第29首写角斗士普里斯库斯与维鲁斯势均力敌，皇帝让两人同时获得解除比斗的木剑", "kind": "事实", "source": "Martial, De Spectaculis 29", "url": "https://pages.pomona.edu/~cmc24747/sources/martial/mart_lib_spect.htm", "year": "约80", "region": "罗马", "freshness": "不适用", "method": ""},
{"id": "F27", "slot": "皇帝落泪", "content": "庆典结束时，提图斯当着民众痛哭。原因史料没有定论", "kind": "事实", "source": "Suetonius, Titus 10 ; Cassius Dio 66.26", "url": "https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Suetonius/12Caesars/Titus*.html ; https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Cassius_Dio/66*.html", "year": "80（庆典末）", "region": "罗马", "freshness": "不适用", "method": ""},
{"id": "F28", "slot": "终点时刻", "content": "提图斯于公元81年9月13日去世，年42岁，死于其父去世的同一处农庄", "kind": "事实", "source": "Suetonius, Titus 11", "url": "https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Suetonius/12Caesars/Titus*.html", "year": "81", "region": "意大利", "freshness": "不适用", "method": ""},

title.final_title: I Time Travelled to the Opening of the Colosseum (80 AD)!
title.viewer_question: 如果我能坐进刚开幕的斗兽场，会看到什么、坐在哪里、是不是一上来就是角斗？
title.expected_answer_direction: 看到角斗士、猛兽、皇帝和狂热的人群
title.fix: 标题不改。正文不承诺确切日期，也不说水战发生在第一天

protagonist.who: 现代来的时间旅行主持人，扮成一个穿深色斗篷、只能坐高处的平民男子
protagonist.place: 罗马，弗拉维圆形剧场（后称斗兽场）
protagonist.source_role: 现代主持人扮成持三等舱船票的泰坦尼克号乘客
protagonist.mapping: 三等舱船票 → 免费入场的座位凭证和高处座位；头等舱 → 元老前排与皇帝包厢；健康检查 → 引座分区；同桌乘客 → 邻座看客；爱尔兰女伴类关键配角 → 虚构的邻座向导；船长 → 皇帝提图斯；冰山警告 → 提醒提图斯他时日无多；4月14日 → 史书那一句注水记载

thesis_card.viewer_belief: 斗兽场从开幕起就是铺着沙子的陆上角斗场，角斗就是它的全部
thesis_card.truth: 卡西乌斯·狄奥写下，提图斯在开幕庆典期间突然把这座竞技场注满了水，放进受过训练的牲畜，还让人乘船打了一场海战
thesis_card.one_line_thesis: 你以为斗兽场的开幕就是沙地上的角斗，可一位罗马史家写下的是：皇帝把整座竞技场注满了水。
thesis_card.ending_landing: 一栋你以为彻底了解的建筑，连开幕庆典里的用法都和你想的不一样。还有几个「当然知道」，你其实从没查过？
thesis_card.differs_from_source_conclusion: 相同点是落在两种「知道」的差别上。不同点是原片比的是读过和活过、落点是哀伤；本片比的是以为知道和查过记载，落点是认知翻转，哀伤只由屠杀和提图斯的结局承担。注水论点由本题自己的狄奥和马提亚尔文本支撑
thesis_card.contrast: 翻案：从干燥的角斗场翻到注水的海战场地
thesis_card.double_standard: 同在一座建筑里看同一场演出，元老坐最靠近场地的前排，穷人和女性只能在最高处
thesis_card.boundary: 只指开幕庆典期间的记载，不代表斗兽场常年办水战；角斗和猎兽同样发生了；苏维托尼乌斯把提图斯的海战记在旧海战池；工程上能否做到仍有争论

facts.content: 卡西乌斯·狄奥记载提图斯开幕庆典期间竞技场被注满水，马、牛等动物在水中表演，人乘船参与水上表演
地下层在约公元80至82年作为第二期工程建成，原设计没有它。开幕时地板下的确切状态，来源没有说明
开幕庆典历时一百多天，约九千只动物被杀，女性也参与了竞技场表演
狄奥《罗马史》66.25：提图斯突然把这座剧场注满水，带入马、牛和受训在水中活动的家畜；又有人乘船扮作科基拉人与科林斯人打海战。狄奥晚于事件一个多世纪写作
狄奥没有说剧场注水是哪一天。他所记「第一天角斗和猎兽、第三天海战」是城外盖乌斯与卢基乌斯林苑一带的场次，那里第一天是在湖面铺木板后举行的
提图斯从高处向剧场里抛刻字小木球，接到的人可兑换食物、衣服、金银器皿、马匹、牲口乃至奴隶
狄奥记有鹤相斗、四头象相斗，约九千只驯养和野生动物被杀，女性参与了宰杀
苏维托尼乌斯把提图斯的模拟海战记在旧海战池，并写到一天之内展示五千只野兽
苏维托尼乌斯记图密善也在圆形剧场里办过海战，因此不能说水战只在开幕时有过
facts.source: Suetonius, Domitian 4（经 Encyclopaedia Romana 引述）

facts.content: 马提亚尔第24首对远道而来的迟到观众说：眼前的水和船别让你误会，这里刚才还是陆地
马提亚尔这组表演诗的成书年代和所指场合有不确定处，有译本题名归到图密善时期
facts.source: Pomona 学院资料页（1897年匿名译本）; Heurist 数据库说明

facts.content: 工程师 Martin Crapper 2007年发表研究认为注水可行，依据包括地下部分抹有灰浆、可能由水道支线供水；场内没有发现水管，供水方案仍属推测
对注满场地所需时间的推算差别很大，从不到一小时到数小时都有，取决于流量和水深假设
有考古学者因缺少管道证据和场地偏小而怀疑；Heinz-Jürgen Beste 认为可能用了专门造的小船。地下层建成后水战难以再办
K. M. Coleman 1993年在 Journal of Roman Studies 讨论早期帝国水上表演，论文结论本次未读到原文
苏维托尼乌斯记奥古斯都时期规定：公共演出首排留给元老，穿深色斗篷者不得坐中部，女性看角斗只能在高处。套用到80年的斗兽场属于推定
看台分为前排台座和其上数层，最高处是木结构廊座，穷人和女性在上面。该木廊在80年是否已完工待查
通行说法是观众凭座位凭证入场，上面标分区、排和座号；80年当时的实物凭证待查
底层80个拱门中76个编号供观众使用，部分编号至今可见，原先涂红
facts.source: 斗兽场考古公园说明牌（HMDB 收录）

facts.content: 阿尔瓦尔祭司团公元80年的石刻记录写明了他们在这座剧场分到的座位空间，现代解读约合37米长
facts.source: the-colosseum.net ; Biblical Archaeology Society 注释（CIL VI 铭文，ILS 5049）

facts.source: Vassar College 学生考古博客（二手，建议再核）

竞技场地面为木板铺沙。开幕时木板下的构造待查
剧场有帆布遮阳篷，由水手操作。80年开幕时的使用情况待查
2022年公布的排水道清理发现无花果、葡萄、橄榄、坚果遗存和熊与大型猫科骨头。这些反映的是剧场长期使用情况，不能定到80年

庆典结束时，提图斯当着民众痛哭。原因史料没有定论
提图斯于公元81年9月13日去世，年42岁，死于其父去世的同一处农庄

title.viewer_question: 如果我能坐进刚开幕的斗兽场，会看到什么、坐在哪里、是不是一上来就是角斗？

protagonist.who: 现代来的时间旅行主持人，扮成一个穿深色斗篷、只能坐高处的平民男子
protagonist.place: 罗马，弗拉维圆形剧场（后称斗兽场）
protagonist.source_role: 现代主持人扮成持三等舱船票的泰坦尼克号乘客
protagonist.mapping: 三等舱船票 → 免费入场的座位凭证和高处座位；头等舱 → 元老前排与皇帝包厢；健康检查 → 引座分区；同桌乘客 → 邻座看客；爱尔兰女伴类关键配角 → 虚构的邻座向导；船长 → 皇帝提图斯；冰山警告 → 提醒提图斯他时日无多；4月14日 → 史书那一句注水记载

thesis_card.viewer_belief: 斗兽场从开幕起就是铺着沙子的陆上角斗场，角斗就是它的全部
thesis_card.truth: 卡西乌斯·狄奥写下，提图斯在开幕庆典期间突然把这座竞技场注满了水，放进受过训练的牲畜，还让人乘船打了一场海战
thesis_card.one_line_thesis: 你以为斗兽场的开幕就是沙地上的角斗，可一位罗马史家写下的是：皇帝把整座竞技场注满了水。
thesis_card.ending_landing: 一栋你以为彻底了解的建筑，连开幕庆典里的用法都和你想的不一样。还有几个「当然知道」，你其实从没查过？
thesis_card.differs_from_source_conclusion: 相同点是落在两种「知道」的差别上。不同点是原片比的是读过和活过、落点是哀伤；本片比的是以为知道和查过记载，落点是认知翻转，哀伤只由屠杀和提图斯的结局承担。注水论点由本题自己的狄奥和马提亚尔文本支撑
thesis_card.contrast: 翻案：从干燥的角斗场翻到注水的海战场地
thesis_card.double_standard: 同在一座建筑里看同一场演出，元老坐最靠近场地的前排，穷人和女性只能在最高处
thesis_card.boundary: 只指开幕庆典期间的记载，不代表斗兽场常年办水战；角斗和猎兽同样发生了；苏维托尼乌斯把提图斯的海战记在旧海战池；工程上能否做到仍有争论

素材声明改为罗马文字记载和现存遗址，不沿用公共领域照片的说法

facts.content: 卡西乌斯·狄奥记载提图斯开幕庆典期间竞技场被注满水，马、牛等动物在水中表演，人乘船参与水上表演
地下层在约公元80至82年作为第二期工程建成，原设计没有它。开幕时地板下的确切状态，来源没有说明
开幕庆典历时一百多天，约九千只动物被杀，女性也参与了竞技场表演
狄奥《罗马史》66.25：提图斯突然把这座剧场注满水，带入马、牛和受训在水中活动的家畜；又有人乘船扮作科基拉人与科林斯人打海战。狄奥晚于事件一个多世纪写作
狄奥没有说剧场注水是哪一天。他所记「第一天角斗和猎兽、第三天海战」是城外盖乌斯与卢基乌斯林苑一带的场次，那里第一天是在湖面铺木板后举行的
提图斯从高处向剧场里抛刻字小木球，接到的人可兑换食物、衣服、金银器皿、马匹、牲口乃至奴隶
狄奥记有鹤相斗、四头象相斗，约九千只驯养和野生动物被杀，女性参与了宰杀
苏维托尼乌斯把提图斯的模拟海战记在旧海战池，并写到一天之内展示五千只野兽
苏维托尼乌斯记图密善也在圆形剧场里办过海战，因此不能说水战只在开幕时有过
facts.source: Suetonius, Domitian 4（经 Encyclopaedia Romana 引述）

facts.content: 马提亚尔第24首对远道而来的迟到观众说：眼前的水和船别让你误会，这里刚才还是陆地
马提亚尔这组表演诗的成书年代和所指场合有不确定处，有译本题名归到图密善时期

facts.content: 工程师 Martin Crapper 2007年发表研究认为注水可行，依据包括地下部分抹有灰浆、可能由水道支线供水；场内没有发现水管，供水方案仍属推测
对注满场地所需时间的推算差别很大，从不到一小时到数小时都有，取决于流量和水深假设
有考古学者因缺少管道证据和场地偏小而怀疑；Heinz-Jürgen Beste 认为可能用了专门造的小船。地下层建成后水战难以再办
K. M. Coleman 1993年在 Journal of Roman Studies 讨论早期帝国水上表演，论文结论本次未读到原文
苏维托尼乌斯记奥古斯都时期规定：公共演出首排留给元老，穿深色斗篷者不得坐中部，女性看角斗只能在高处。套用到80年的斗兽场属于推定
看台分为前排台座和其上数层，最高处是木结构廊座，穷人和女性在上面。该木廊在80年是否已完工待查
通行说法是观众凭座位凭证入场，上面标分区、排和座号；80年当时的实物凭证待查
底层80个拱门中76个编号供观众使用，部分编号至今可见，原先涂红

source_chain.main_why: 观众早知道结局是灾难，一直看下去主要是在乎主角能不能闯进禁区、警告有没有用、灾难到来时她和身边的人会怎样，舱内见闻是挂在这条结局线上的填充和奖励。
source_chain.voiced_style: 很少用问句，多在开头和转段处用「我要做什么」「今晚会有什么」「明天是什么日子」这类目标宣告和预告把张力挑明，段内靠见闻和事件推进。
source_chain.big_tension: 明知这个世界注定毁灭，一个闯入其中的知情者能走到多深、能不能改变结局、又要怎样面对眼前这些人的命运？

segments.open_abs: 一个知情者以很低的身份进入注定出事的地方，会经历什么？
segments.payoff: 地点、日期、身份和票价一次交代清楚，随即宣布要想办法进头等舱。
segments.raises: 三等舱的她能不能混进头等舱？
segments.raises_abs: 身份不够的人能不能闯进不许她进的地方？
segments.voiced_line: 虽然拿的是三等舱票，但我肯定还是要想办法进头等舱。

segments.open_abs: 我看到的这个世界有多接近真实？
segments.payoff: 说明画面由公有领域的真实插图和照片转化而来，尽量贴近原貌。
segments.raises: 按真实资料复原的船上世界到底长什么样？
segments.raises_abs: 这个尽力还原的世界里面是什么样子？

segments.raises: 她的冰山警告能不能传到船长那里，有没有用？
segments.raises_abs: 知情者能不能阻止那场注定的灾难？
segments.voiced_line: 我想试着跟船长说冰山的事，总得有人至少试着说点什么。

segments.open: 登船检查在查什么，她过得去吗？
segments.open_abs: 进门的第一道关卡，她能不能通过？
segments.payoff: 原来是健康检查，她通过了；同时看到头等舱乘客直接上船，而三等舱走廊比预想的好得多。
segments.raises: 三等舱的住处和生活到底是什么条件？
segments.raises_abs: 底层身份在里面过的是什么日子？

segments.open: 三等舱的房间、床和厕所到底怎么样？
segments.open_abs: 底层的日常条件到底如何？
segments.payoff: 床单干净、有自来水，但床太短、厕所在船尾；随后船启航了。
segments.raises: 船开了，同行的是些什么人，吃的又怎么样？
segments.raises_abs: 真正上路之后，身边是谁，日子怎么过？

segments.open: 同船的人为什么上船，三等舱的饭好不好吃？
segments.open_abs: 这里的普通人怀着什么期待，过着怎样的生活？
segments.payoff: 同桌人讲了到纽约后的打算；米汤寡淡，但面包蘸汤和布丁出乎意料地好；听说晚上公共舱有演奏。
segments.raises: 今晚的三等舱聚会会热闹成什么样？
segments.raises_abs: 底层人的狂欢之夜会是什么样？

segments.open: 这场聚会上会发生什么，她能融进去吗？
segments.open_abs: 主角能不能融入这群人，会遇到谁？
segments.payoff: 她跟着乱跳、玩得很开心，认识了 Liam，随后把他叫到外面说有话要坦白。
segments.raises: 她要向这个刚认识的人坦白什么，对方会怎么反应？
segments.raises_abs: 主角要向新结识的人交底，后果会怎样？
segments.voiced_line: 我有件事得告诉你，出来一下。

segments.open: 坦白身份之后他会怎么反应，她能借此进头等舱吗？
segments.open_abs: 交出秘密能不能换来进入禁区的路？
segments.payoff: 她自称来自2026年，Liam 指出一道有短暂无人看守空档的门；她换装赶过去，成功进入并道别。
segments.raises: 门那边的头等舱是什么样，跟下面差多少？
segments.raises_abs: 禁区里面到底是什么样的世界？

segments.open_abs: 上层世界和底层到底差多少？
segments.payoff: 厚地毯、真木料、大楼梯与三等舱形成强烈反差；乘客礼貌而冷淡。
segments.raises: 她本不该在这里，还能看到哪些地方，会不会露馅？
segments.raises_abs: 闯入者还能走多深，会不会被识破？

segments.open: 头等舱还有什么，她能看到多少？
segments.open_abs: 上层世界的享受还能到什么程度？
segments.payoff: 看到十一道菜的晚宴、女性不能进的吸烟室和寒冷而美丽的甲板夜景，然后点出明天就是4月14日。
segments.raises: 沉船的日子到了，这一切繁华和这些人会怎样？
segments.raises_abs: 灾难日期逼近，眼前的美好会怎样收场？
segments.voiced_line: 我已经在船上三晚了，明天是4月14日。

segments.open: 出事的这一天到了，她打算怎么办？
segments.open_abs: 大限当天，知情者要做什么？
segments.payoff: 她说出对认识的人的牵挂，决定趁船长今晚赴宴时去警告他。
segments.raises: 她能不能混进去拦到船长？这是唯一的机会。

segments.voiced_line: 今晚的晚宴是我最好、也是唯一真正的机会。

segments.open: 她准备怎么说、在哪里堵船长，能等到吗？
segments.open_abs: 行动计划是什么，能不能顺利执行？
segments.payoff: 排练好说辞，算好船长大约九点离席，穿着沉重礼服守在门口，终于开口拦住他。
segments.raises: 船长听了会不会相信、会不会减速？

segments.voiced_line: 我要告诉他今晚冰山风险很大，强烈建议天黑后减速。

segments.payoff: 船长礼貌地说已收到多份冰情警告、高级船员在监视；她承认没劝动，但试过了。
segments.raises: 警告失败了，漆黑的海上，撞击什么时候来？
segments.raises_abs: 阻止不了之后，灾难会怎样降临？

segments.open: 撞击那一刻会是什么样，船上的人会察觉吗？
segments.open_abs: 注定的时刻到来时，身在其中的人什么反应？
segments.payoff: 11点38分起倒数，冰山出现、转舵不及；多数人几乎没感觉，有人认为没什么大事，船员开始让人穿救生衣。
segments.raises: 这些还不当回事的人，接下来会怎样？
segments.raises_abs: 还没意识到危险的人，何时醒悟、结局如何？

segments.raises: 留在船上的人和她认识的那些人，最后怎么样了？

question_chain.mode_why: 原片靠「闯进去的人后来怎样」推进，让观众以穿越者身份进斗兽场，最能把座位等级、开幕见闻和那条有争议的水战记载串成一条线。
question_chain.setup: 假设你是一个26岁的现代人，穿越到公元80年斗兽场开幕庆典期间的罗马，在当地人眼里只是一个没身份、没靠山的外来女子。
question_chain.big_question: 斗兽场开幕的时候，场上真的只是一片沙地和角斗士厮杀吗？

cases_use.name: 百年后的记录者(卡西乌斯·狄奥，晚于事件一个多世纪的罗马史家)
cases_use.as: 反转：他写下剧场被注满水，推翻「开幕只有沙地」的印象；同时交代他写作时间晚

cases_use.name: 迟到观众诗人(马提亚尔，写诗称颂皇帝表演的罗马诗人)
cases_use.as: 证据：他写给迟到观众的话，用来呈现水面出现后的反差，并说明诗的场合有不确定处

cases_use.name: 打平的两个人(角斗士普里斯库斯与维鲁斯)
cases_use.as: 真故事：在大量死亡之后，出现两个人一起活着离场的时刻

cases_use.name: 落泪的皇帝(皇帝提图斯，开幕庆典的主办者)
cases_use.as: 情绪余韵：庆典结束时当众痛哭，原因没有定论，次年去世

questions.ask: 你这样一个没身份的人进了斗兽场，能靠场地多近？
questions.answer: 按座位规矩，你多半只能待在最高处，是离场地最远的那一层。

questions.ask: 那么远，你就这么认了？
questions.answer: 不认。你给自己定下目标：混进不许你去的地方，下到靠近场边的前排。

questions.ask: 冒着被赶出去的险下去，你到底图什么？
questions.answer: 图亲眼核对一件事：照片和电影里的那片沙地，开幕时是不是真的就是这样。能不能下去、会看到什么，此刻你都不知道。

questions.ask: 我接下来看到的这些，有多少是真的？
questions.answer: 有史料或考古依据的照实讲，说法不一的（比如场地下面当时的构造）会点明；穿越身份、向导、潜入和对话是虚构，在这里统一交代。画面素材和制作方法须由制作方确认后才能写。

questions.ask: 既然来了，你打算做成哪几件事？
questions.answer: 看清入场、座位、观众和场地，还要做一件更难的事：给主办庆典的皇帝提图斯身边的人递个话。你知道他在第二年，也就是公元81年就会去世。

questions.ask: 第一关，你进得去吗？
questions.answer: 进得去：入场免费，通行说法是凭座位凭证（80年的实物待查），从编号拱门进场。抬头看到刻出并涂红的门号，里面是常见估计约五万人的巨大看台。

questions.ask: 最高处的穷人座位，待着到底是什么滋味？
questions.answer: 穷人和女性在最上层，离场地远得像现代球场的最后一排；木廊座当时是否完工还不确定。馆内设有饮水泉和厕所，但开幕时是否启用不明。

questions.ask: 挤在你身边的是些什么人，他们在盼什么？
questions.answer: 有诗里写到的远方来客，也有带着吃食的普通人（无花果、葡萄、坚果的遗存来自长期使用，不能定到80年）。大家盼的是皇帝抛下刻字小木球，接到就能兑换东西。

questions.ask: 木球扔下来的那一刻，看台会变成什么样？
questions.answer: 提图斯从高处抛球，看台瞬间乱成一团：球能换食物、衣服、金银器皿乃至牲口和奴隶，一颗小木球里可能装着另一个人的命运，人人都在扑。

questions.ask: 这么乱，你抢到了吗，有没有惹出麻烦？
questions.answer: 邻座的女人帮你抢到一颗，可她也看出你不对劲，要你私下说清楚来历。

questions.ask: 跟她说实话，会害了你还是帮到你？
questions.answer: 你坦白自己来自未来，她告诉你一条通往前排的路和一小段可混过去的时间。你装成有资格的人下去，终于站到了靠近场地的地方。

questions.ask: 前排和楼上到底差多少？
questions.answer: 靠场地最近的座位留给元老，有的祭司团连分到多长一段座位都刻在石头上。在这里能看清木板铺沙的场地，看清鹤相斗、四头象相斗，而脚下那层木板下面还有空间。

questions.ask: 这场庆典还能夸张到什么地步？
questions.answer: 庆典长达一百天，而最惊人的是史家卡西乌斯·狄奥后来写下的一笔：提图斯突然把整座剧场注满水，放进受过训练、能在水里活动的动物，还让人乘船打海战。

questions.ask: 等等，我眼前这片沙地，真会变成水面？
questions.answer: 你读过的记载是这么写的，可此刻场上还是干的沙子。会不会亲眼见到，只能等。

questions.ask: 如果水真要来，你现在该做什么？
questions.answer: 哪一天注水史料没说，剧情里邻座打听到就是今天。全场只有你读过后来的记载，也只有你知道皇帝剩下的时间不多，递话必须赶在场面开始之前。

questions.ask: 动手之前先想清楚，那条注水的记载靠得住吗？
questions.answer: 有三处疑点：狄奥晚了一个多世纪才写；苏维托尼乌斯把提图斯的模拟海战记在旧海战池；供水怎样接入没有考古证据，地下结构也有分歧。但也有工程研究认为注水可行。（本段改用「想知道」，因为要正面摆证据。）

questions.ask: 你的警告，皇帝那边的人听得进去吗？
questions.answer: 你趁那段时间窗找到提图斯的随从，提醒皇帝可能活不过明年，对方听完，客气地把你请开。

questions.ask: 还能再试一次吗？
questions.answer: 不能了，时间窗已过。你试过了，话没递进去，只能回到场边看着那片场地。

questions.ask: 那片沙地，到底有没有变成水面？
questions.answer: 在这趟旅程里变了：水一点点漫上来，船进了场，扮作两方打起海战；马提亚尔写诗提醒迟到者，这里刚才还是陆地（诗的场合有不确定处）。现代推算注水要半小时左右到几个小时，具体过程是复原想象。

questions.ask: 这一百天热闹下来，付出了什么，又是怎么收场的？
questions.answer: 狄奥记剧场与浴场落成庆典中约九千只动物被杀；场上也有普里斯库斯与维鲁斯打成平手、双双获得木剑。可到庆典结束时，提图斯当众痛哭，原因没有定论，次年他就去世了。

questions.ask: 走完这一趟，你要核对的事有结果了吗：开幕只有沙地和角斗？
questions.answer: 不只是。有人写过它装满水、打过海战，斗兽场考古公园官网也认可开幕海战；但是否发生、怎样做到，学界仍有争论。

questions.ask: 亲身走过一遭，你的看法变了什么？
questions.answer: 你原以为认得这座建筑，其实只是认得它的样子：认得一栋建筑和查过它，是两回事。

questions.ask: 回到现代，再看见斗兽场，你会想起什么？
questions.answer: 今天露出的砖石地下迷宫并不是公元80年的模样。下次在照片或电影里看见斗兽场的沙地，你会想起有人写过它装满水的样子。

opening.hook: 一提斗兽场，你想到的多半是一片沙地，两个人拿着武器拼命。可它刚开门的时候，场上发生的事可能远不是这么简单。
opening.who: 你26岁，从现代穿越到公元80年的罗马，正赶上这座新剧场的开幕庆典；在这里你是一个没身份、没靠山的外来女子。
opening.link: 你对斗兽场的全部印象都来自照片和电影，这次是亲自来核对它开幕时到底是什么样。
opening.want: 你最想走到场边亲眼看清那块场地，最怕身份被识破，被人赶出去。

[CH01 | 0:00-1:00 | 瞬间落地、立下身位与越界目标、交代虚实边界、挂出探索与提醒两条任务]
Okay, so that is the Colosseum, brand new. This is Rome in AD 80, where the emperor throws little wooden balls into the crowd, and one can get you a horse. I’m in a dark cloak, way up at the back. I’m 26, from today, a nobody, an outsider woman. My seat’s free. The front is for senators. Obviously, I am going to try to get to the front row anyway. I want that ground up close. Getting thrown out scares me. For now, the top. Here we go.

[PENDING PRODUCER CONFIRMATION] I used Roman writings and standing ruins to rebuild this world.

Where historians argue, I’ll tell you. My time travel, guide, sneaking and conversations are invented.

[PENDING PRODUCER CONFIRMATION] Enjoy, guys. This was a lot of work.

If you know this place from films, like me, the surprise isn’t who fights. It’s what happens to the ground under them.

Just between you and me: senators’ seats, emperor’s box, the sand. I want to get close. I also want to warn Emperor Titus. He dies next year. First, can I even get in? Wish me luck.

[CH02 | 1:00-1:55 | 用入场关卡让阶层制度第一次显形，并给一个意料之外的视觉细节]
Yes, I can get in. My stomach just doesn’t believe it yet.

I’m in line, hood low. Please don’t ask me anything. I’m holding a seat token with my section, row and seat. That’s how it’s usually told, anyway. No real one from this opening year is confirmed.

And the price? Nothing. Free.

Then comes the catch. Free doesn’t mean sit wherever you like. Your place in society picks your seat. I look like a nobody, so I’m going up.

Wait. Look at that.

A number, cut into the stone. Painted red. It really jumps out. The crowd comes in through 76 numbered arches. You can still see 29 of those numbers on the north side today.

I step through and look up. Oh. People everywhere. A common estimate says this place holds about 50,000.

And I’m headed for the very top. What’s it actually like in the poor seats?

[CH03 | 1:55-2:55 | 用身体感受建立真实感，用现代参照制造幽默，考据不确定处点明]
Tight. That’s the first thing.

My legs are done with stairs. I squeeze in sideways. One shoulder on my left, one elbow on my right. I lean forward to find the field. There it is. Tiny.

You know the last row of a stadium, where you just watch the big screen? This is that row. No screen.

There’s a rule behind this. A Roman writer says Augustus, an earlier emperor, sent women up high for gladiator fights. Dark cloaks couldn’t sit in the middle. Applying that here is an inference. Still, I tick both boxes.

Women and the poor get the top, a wooden gallery. In our reconstruction, I’m in it. Was it really finished by opening day? Not confirmed.

Shade would be lovely. This building had a canvas awning, worked by sailors. Whether they used it at the opening isn’t confirmed either.

Thirsty? Archaeologists believe there were drinking fountains and toilets. How many, where, and whether they worked yet, nobody knows. I’m holding everything in.

Then the woman beside me shifts to make room. Who are all these people, and what are they waiting for?

[CH04 | 2:55-4:05 | 把普通观众人化，给食物考据细节，并预告即将发生的集体活动]
“First time here?” she asks.

Her name is Tullia. She sells lamp wicks, she has shut her stall for the day, and she is not going home empty-handed. Her words.

“And you’re from where?”

“North,” I say. “Very north.”

My accent is strange. I’m sitting too stiffly. She notices both.

Luckily, strange has company up here. A Roman poet, Martial, wrote that people came to Rome to watch from Thrace and Sarmatia, from Arabia and Ethiopia. It’s one man’s poem praising the show. But I’m clinging to it. Maybe I’m just one more foreigner.

Tullia offers me a fig. People around us are nibbling, and you’d recognize the menu. Figs, grapes, olives, nuts. Remains of all four turned up when the drains here were cleared, in finds announced in 2022. So did bones from bears and big cats. But that mess built up over many years of use. None of it can be pinned to this opening.

I reach for another fig. Tullia catches my wrist.

“Keep your hands empty,” she says, and nods toward the emperor. “He’s going to throw the balls.”

Heads are turning his way, all along our row. Somebody in this crowd is going home with the good one. What happens to these seats when those little balls come down?

[CH05 | 4:05-5:20 | 集体高光，收束上一章活动悬念，配角起疑并发出私下谈话邀约]
They explode.

A little wooden ball is already dropping from on high, and our whole row lunges for it. I jump. I miss. I get an elbow, a stomped toe and a face full of somebody’s sleeve. We came from all over, and now we’re all making the same greedy face. I can’t stop laughing.

Cassius Dio, a Roman historian writing more than a century later, says the emperor threw these balls, each one marked with writing. Catch one and trade it in. Food. Clothing. Gold and silver vessels. Horses. Cattle.

And slaves.

I stop laughing. That’s a person. One of these little things, bouncing off people’s fingers, can hand a human being to a stranger. People are still grabbing. My arms stay down.

Then something hard hits my palm. Tullia has scooped up a ball and closed my fingers around it.

“Yours,” she says. “Now bring on Priscus and Verus.”

Two gladiators. The poet Martial wrote about them, and people here can’t wait.

Then she looks at me, really looks. “You catch like you’ve never had hands,” she says. “And that’s no northern accent.” Her voice drops. “Behind that post. Tell me where you’re really from.”

Will the truth sink me or save me?

[CH06 | 5:20-6:40 | 向配角坦白身份换取路线情报，限时伪装完成层级突破]
It saves me. But first there’s a horrible silence.

We’re squeezed behind the post, and I just say it. “I’m not from the north. I’m from the future. I haven’t been born yet, and I won’t be for a very long time.”

Tullia doesn’t blink. I wait for her to yell for an usher. Instead she asks, “Do people there still buy wicks?”

“Loads,” I lie.

She nods, very pleased. “And what does someone from the future want?”

“To see that sand up close.”

She counts my problems on her fingers. Dark cloak: not even allowed in the middle seats. Woman: stuck up high for gladiators. That’s the old Augustus rule, if it holds here. And the very front? Senators.

Then she pulls off her pale wrap.

“Wear this. I keep your cloak. Take the side stairs down, then the passage toward the front. Walk like someone sent you.” She points at a strip of sunlight on the wall below. “When that’s gone, so are you. After that, the man watching the gap will be back.”

So here I am, 26, in a borrowed wrap, a wooden ball in my fist, heading where I have no right to be.

Halfway down, a doorkeeper puts out his arm. “Who are you with?”

My mouth goes dry. “Message,” I say, and point ahead like it’s urgent. He studies the wrap. Someone shouts behind him. He turns, and I slip past.

I don’t sit. I don’t dare. But I’m standing at the edge of the senators’ section, right by the field.

How different is it down here?

[CH07 | 6:40-7:55 | 禁区奇观与阶层硬对照，中点观众自测，埋下脚下这层地面的疑问]
Completely. Oh my god. Look at the room they have.

I stay tucked against the end wall, trying to look like furniture. These closest places are for senators. Upstairs I had an elbow in my ribs. Down here a man can spread his arms.

And rank gets measured. A group of priests, the Arval Brethren, had their share of this theatre cut into stone in AD 80. Modern scholars read it as about 37 meters of seating. That’s roughly 120 feet, in writing. My share was half a squeeze.

Then the field. It was tiny from the top. Now it’s everything.

Cranes are fighting, all wings and legs. Then elephants. Four of them, going at each other, so close I feel it in my knees. Dio lists both for these games, though putting them on today is our reconstruction. The man nearest me is picking his teeth.

An elephant skids, and the sand scrapes away. Wood. The floor is planks with sand spread on top, and there’s space underneath. What exactly was built down there at the opening, historians still disagree.

So take a guess with me. You’ve got sand, boards and a hollow space below. What happens to this floor before these games are over? Does it stay the way it looks now? Hold on to your answer.

How much wilder can this festival get?

[CH08 | 7:55-9:05 | 用本题史料推翻对场地的既有认知，并挂起是否亲眼见到的倒计时悬念]
A lot wilder. This party runs for 100 days.

Elephants, a few steps away, and the man beside me is asking his friend about dinner. My heart is still pounding.

And now I have to tell you what I read before I came. Cassius Dio wrote that Titus suddenly filled this very theatre with water. He brought in horses, bulls and other tame animals that had been trained to move in it. Then came people on ships, fighting a sea battle as two Greek sides, the Corcyraeans and the Corinthians. Remember, Dio wrote this more than a century later.

That’s the surprise I promised you. It was never about who fights. In his account, the ground itself disappears.

This ground. The one right here.

I look down. Dry. Completely dry. A puff of dust hangs where the elephant slid. People are chatting, stretching, craning to see what’s next. Not one of them is looking at the floor.

I am. There’s space under those boards. Is that where water would go? Where would it even come from?

Nobody has written Dio’s sentence yet. I’ve read it. My strip of sunlight is getting thinner, and I can’t tell whether I’ll see this sand turn into water. All I can do is wait and watch.

Or is it? If the water really is coming, what should I do now?

[CH09 | 9:05-9:40 | 调性由轻转重，确立唯一知情者与紧迫感]
Warn him. Before it starts.

People are cheering. I can’t. I don’t want this day to go on.

Tullia has crept to the foot of the stairs. “I asked around,” she whispers. “The water is today.”

I only have her word. Dio names no day for it. His day-by-day schedule belongs to another venue, outside the city.

No one around me has his account. I’m alone with it, and with the date Titus dies: next year.

Before I risk this, can I trust that account?

[CH10 | 9:40-10:55 | 把反对证据和支持理由逐一正面摆出，同时彩排要说的话]
Not completely.

I edge along the wall toward the emperor’s box, rehearsing. “Caesar, take care of your health.” Under that, I’m arguing with myself.

Dio wrote late. Another Roman writer, Suetonius, puts Titus’s mock sea battle somewhere else, in an old naval basin. Martial’s show poems mention water, but their date and occasion are uncertain.

Still, it may be possible. A 2007 study by engineer Martin Crapper argued the arena could be filled. He pointed to plaster lining underground and a possible branch from an aqueduct.

But no archaeological evidence shows how that supply got in or was controlled. Modern estimates for filling run from about half an hour to several hours. That’s an awkward fit for “suddenly.”

Some scholars doubt it, pointing to missing pipes and a small arena. Heinz-Jürgen Beste suggests specially built small boats may have been used.

Even the space under the boards is disputed. The site’s official park says it was wood at the opening. Others say it was built later.

So it could have happened. I can’t call it proven.

[CH09 | 9:05-9:40 | 调性由轻转重，确立唯一知情者与紧迫感]
It has to be now. This is the closest I will ever stand to anyone around the emperor. Once that doorkeeper is back, my free run is over.

Then something changes on the field. The animals are being driven off. The gates at one end swing wide, and in the dark behind them I make out a high, curved shape. Is that the front of a boat?

My feet won’t move. If I stay here, I have the best view in the building of whatever comes next.

Around me, people cheer. Titus laughs at something. He has no idea what I know about next year.

I peel myself off the wall and start walking. But what if the water I’m giving up was never going to come?

[CH10 | 9:40-10:55 | 把反对证据和支持理由逐一正面摆出，同时彩排要说的话]
It might not. I edge along the passage, arguing with myself.

First, Dio wrote late, more than a century after this day. And out of 100 days of festival, he never says which one got the water. I duck behind a man carrying a tray.

Second, another Roman writer, Suetonius, puts Titus’s mock sea battle somewhere else, in an old basin built for naval shows. “Caesar,” I rehearse under my breath, “take care of your health.” Too vague. I try again.

Third, could the building even do it? An engineer, Martin Crapper, argued in 2007 that it could, with water possibly branching off an aqueduct. But no archaeological evidence shows how that water got in or was controlled. Some scholars doubt the whole thing.

Those boards with the hollow space under them? Even they’re part of the fight. The park says timber came first, and brick arrived under a later emperor, Domitian. Others say nothing was built down there until his reign.

So it could have happened. I can’t call it proven.

The box is right above me now. The sunlight on the wall is down to a sliver. “Caesar,” I whisper, one last time, “please be careful.”

Will anyone near him listen?

[CH11 | 10:55-11:30 | 干预被客气挡下，任务以尽力而无效收束]
An attendant steps into my path below the box.

“Please,” I say. “Tell the emperor to take care of himself. He may not live past next year.”

Above us, Titus is still talking, close enough that I can see his mouth move. He never looks down.

The attendant listens to every word. “Caesar thanks you for your concern,” he says gently. “This way, please.”

His hand turns me around. I try once more over my shoulder, but the crowd roars and swallows it. He walks me back along the passage and leaves me there.

The strip of sun is gone. The doorkeeper is back, filling the doorway. Behind him stands Tullia, waiting for her wrap. He looks at me and doesn’t move an inch. No way out, and no way back to the box.

I tried. All that’s left is the end wall and the field.

So does that sand become water?

[CH12 | 11:30-12:30 | 按进程呈现场面发生，旁观者的轻松反衬知情者的沉重，回收沙地埋点]
It does, in this journey.

Those boards and the hollow space under them are about to matter. First the sand darkens along the edge. Then it shines. Puddles find each other. A line of hoofprints softens, fills and vanishes. The noise of the crowd drops, then comes back twice as loud. The ground I came to see slides out of sight. Remember your guess?

Then the animals come in. Horses wade out with their heads high, snorting at the splashes. Bulls follow, shoulders pushing the water into little waves. They’ve been trained for this, and they move through it as if someone had simply flooded their field.

And then the ships. The shape behind the gate was a bow. It noses out into the light, and more follow, oars dipping. Men crowd the decks. One side plays the Corcyraeans, the other the Corinthians, two Greek peoples fighting all over again, here in the middle of Rome.

They close in. Oars clatter against oars. Wood knocks on wood. A man leaps across the gap, nearly misses, and gets hauled up by his belt. Spray reaches the front seats, and a senator wipes his face, delighted.

Martial has words for anyone arriving late: don’t let the water and the boats fool you. A moment ago, this was land.

Filling it for real would have taken from about half an hour to several hours, and even the occasion of Martial’s poem is uncertain, but here I am, watching the floor of the Colosseum ripple.

“See?” Tullia calls past the doorkeeper. “Good show.”

A hundred days of this. What does it cost, and how does it end?

[CH13 | 12:30-13:15 | 呈现庆典的代价与见证者决堤，以无解的情绪事件留余韵]
When the boats are gone, I see killing.

One crane keeps trying to stand. One wing drags in the sand. It gets halfway up, folds, and tries again. I can’t look at anything else.

Dio puts the animal dead at about 9,000, tame and wild. That’s his total for this theatre and the new public baths together. Some women of low standing helped with the killing.

Behind the doorkeeper, Tullia has a fig halfway to her mouth. She’s watching the crane too. Slowly, she lowers her hand. This time she doesn’t call it a good show.

Then come two gladiators, the pair she was waiting for, Priscus and Verus. In Martial’s poem, neither can beat the other. Titus gives them both the wooden sword that releases a fighter. Two men go in, and two men walk out. Tullia is shouting herself hoarse, and so am I.

My journey jumps to the last of the hundred days. Titus is crying, openly, in front of his people. The old writers leave no settled reason. In September of the next year, at 41, he’ll be dead.

So did I get my answer? Was it only sand and gladiators?

[CH14 | 13:15-14:00 | 回答标题，给出主题对照判断，用建筑现状回扣开头]
No. On the page, at least, the opening was more than sand and gladiators.

Back in my own time, I’m looking down at a maze of bare brick. This isn’t what lay under the floor in AD 80. I miss the noise. I miss the smell of wet sand. And somewhere in my head, Tullia still wants her wrap back.

Everyone pictures the Colosseum as a sandy arena. I did too. So the next time you see that sand in a photo or a film, remember that someone once wrote of it filled with water.

Recognizing a building and checking it are two different things.

versions.text:
[CH01 | 0:00-1:00 | 瞬间落地、立下身位与越界目标、交代虚实边界、挂出探索与提醒两条任务]
Okay, so that is the Colosseum, brand new. This is Rome in AD 80, where the emperor throws little wooden balls into the crowd, and one can get you a horse. I’m in a dark cloak, way up at the back. I’m 26, from today, a nobody, an outsider woman. My seat’s free. The front is for senators. Obviously, I am going to try to get to the front row anyway. I want that ground up close. Getting thrown out scares me. For now, the top. Here we go.

[PENDING PRODUCER CONFIRMATION] I used Roman writings and standing ruins to rebuild this world.

Where historians argue, I’ll tell you. My time travel, guide, sneaking and conversations are invented.

[PENDING PRODUCER CONFIRMATION] Enjoy, guys. This was a lot of work.

If you know this place from films, like me, the surprise isn’t who fights. It’s what happens to the ground under them.

Just between you and me: senators’ seats, emperor’s box, the sand. I want to get close. I also want to warn Emperor Titus. He dies next year. First, can I even get in? Wish me luck.

[CH02 | 1:00-1:55 | 用入场关卡让阶层制度第一次显形，并给一个意料之外的视觉细节]
Yes, I can get in. My stomach just doesn’t believe it yet.

I’m in line, hood low. Please don’t ask me anything. I’m holding a seat token with my section, row and seat. That’s how it’s usually told, anyway. No real one from this opening year is confirmed.

And the price? Nothing. Free.

Then comes the catch. Free doesn’t mean sit wherever you like. Your place in society picks your seat. I look like a nobody, so I’m going up.

Wait. Look at that.

A number, cut into the stone. Painted red. It really jumps out. The crowd comes in through 76 numbered arches. You can still see 29 of those numbers on the north side today.

I step through and look up. Oh. People everywhere. A common estimate says this place holds about 50,000.

And I’m headed for the very top. What’s it actually like in the poor seats?

[CH03 | 1:55-2:55 | 用身体感受建立真实感，用现代参照制造幽默，考据不确定处点明]
Tight. That’s the first thing.

My legs are done with stairs. I squeeze in sideways. One shoulder on my left, one elbow on my right. I lean forward to find the field. There it is. Tiny.

You know the last row of a stadium, where you just watch the big screen? This is that row. No screen.

There’s a rule behind this. A Roman writer says Augustus, an earlier emperor, sent women up high for gladiator fights. Dark cloaks couldn’t sit in the middle. Applying that here is an inference. Still, I tick both boxes.

Women and the poor get the top, a wooden gallery. In our reconstruction, I’m in it. Was it really finished by opening day? Not confirmed.

Shade would be lovely. This building had a canvas awning, worked by sailors. Whether they used it at the opening isn’t confirmed either.

Thirsty? Archaeologists believe there were drinking fountains and toilets. How many, where, and whether they worked yet, nobody knows. I’m holding everything in.

Then the woman beside me shifts to make room. Who are all these people, and what are they waiting for?

[CH04 | 2:55-4:05 | 把普通观众人化，给食物考据细节，并预告即将发生的集体活动]
“First time here?” she asks.

Her name is Tullia. She sells lamp wicks, she has shut her stall for the day, and she is not going home empty-handed. Her words.

“And you’re from where?”

“North,” I say. “Very north.”

My accent is strange. I’m sitting too stiffly. She notices both.

Luckily, strange has company up here. A Roman poet, Martial, wrote that people came to Rome to watch from Thrace and Sarmatia, from Arabia and Ethiopia. It’s one man’s poem praising the show. But I’m clinging to it. Maybe I’m just one more foreigner.

Tullia offers me a fig. People around us are nibbling, and you’d recognize the menu. Figs, grapes, olives, nuts. Remains of all four turned up when the drains here were cleared, in finds announced in 2022. So did bones from bears and big cats. But that mess built up over many years of use. None of it can be pinned to this opening.

I reach for another fig. Tullia catches my wrist.

“Keep your hands empty,” she says, and nods toward the emperor. “He’s going to throw the balls.”

Heads are turning his way, all along our row. Somebody in this crowd is going home with the good one. What happens to these seats when those little balls come down?

[CH05 | 4:05-5:20 | 集体高光，收束上一章活动悬念，配角起疑并发出私下谈话邀约]
They explode.

A little wooden ball is already dropping from on high, and our whole row lunges for it. I jump. I miss. I get an elbow, a stomped toe and a face full of somebody’s sleeve. We came from all over, and now we’re all making the same greedy face. I can’t stop laughing.

Cassius Dio, a Roman historian writing more than a century later, says the emperor threw these balls, each one marked with writing. Catch one and trade it in. Food. Clothing. Gold and silver vessels. Horses. Cattle.

And slaves.

I stop laughing. That’s a person. One of these little things, bouncing off people’s fingers, can hand a human being to a stranger. People are still grabbing. My arms stay down.

Then something hard hits my palm. Tullia has scooped up a ball and closed my fingers around it.

“Yours,” she says. “Now bring on Priscus and Verus.”

Two gladiators. The poet Martial wrote about them, and people here can’t wait.

Then she looks at me, really looks. “You catch like you’ve never had hands,” she says. “And that’s no northern accent.” Her voice drops. “Behind that post. Tell me where you’re really from.”

Will the truth sink me or save me?

[CH06 | 5:20-6:40 | 向配角坦白身份换取路线情报，限时伪装完成层级突破]
It saves me. But first there’s a horrible silence.

We’re squeezed behind the post, and I just say it. “I’m not from the north. I’m from the future. I haven’t been born yet, and I won’t be for a very long time.”

Tullia doesn’t blink. I wait for her to yell for an usher. Instead she asks, “Do people there still buy wicks?”

“Loads,” I lie.

She nods, very pleased. “And what does someone from the future want?”

“To see that sand up close.”

She counts my problems on her fingers. Dark cloak: not even allowed in the middle seats. Woman: stuck up high for gladiators. That’s the old Augustus rule, if it holds here. And the very front? Senators.

Then she pulls off her pale wrap.

“Wear this. I keep your cloak. Take the side stairs down, then the passage toward the front. Walk like someone sent you.” She points at a strip of sunlight on the wall below. “When that’s gone, so are you. After that, the man watching the gap will be back.”

So here I am, 26, in a borrowed wrap, a wooden ball in my fist, heading where I have no right to be.

Halfway down, a doorkeeper puts out his arm. “Who are you with?”

My mouth goes dry. “Message,” I say, and point ahead like it’s urgent. He studies the wrap. Someone shouts behind him. He turns, and I slip past.

I don’t sit. I don’t dare. But I’m standing at the edge of the senators’ section, right by the field.

How different is it down here?

[CH07 | 6:40-7:55 | 禁区奇观与阶层硬对照，中点观众自测，埋下脚下这层地面的疑问]
Completely. Oh my god. Look at the room they have.

I stay tucked against the end wall, trying to look like furniture. These closest places are for senators. Upstairs I had an elbow in my ribs. Down here a man can spread his arms.

And rank gets measured. A group of priests, the Arval Brethren, had their share of this theatre cut into stone in AD 80. Modern scholars read it as about 37 meters of seating. That’s roughly 120 feet, in writing. My share was half a squeeze.

Then the field. It was tiny from the top. Now it’s everything.

Cranes are fighting, all wings and legs. Then elephants. Four of them, going at each other, so close I feel it in my knees. Dio lists both for these games, though putting them on today is our reconstruction. The man nearest me is picking his teeth.

An elephant skids, and the sand scrapes away. Wood. The floor is planks with sand spread on top, and there’s space underneath. What exactly was built down there at the opening, historians still disagree.

So take a guess with me. You’ve got sand, boards and a hollow space below. What happens to this floor before these games are over? Does it stay the way it looks now? Hold on to your answer.

How much wilder can this festival get?

[CH08 | 7:55-9:05 | 用本题史料推翻对场地的既有认知，并挂起是否亲眼见到的倒计时悬念]
A lot wilder. This party runs for 100 days.

Elephants, a few steps away, and the man beside me is asking his friend about dinner. My heart is still pounding.

And now I have to tell you what I read before I came. Cassius Dio wrote that Titus suddenly filled this very theatre with water. He brought in horses, bulls and other tame animals that had been trained to move in it. Then came people on ships, fighting a sea battle as two Greek sides, the Corcyraeans and the Corinthians. Remember, Dio wrote this more than a century later.

That’s the surprise I promised you. It was never about who fights. In his account, the ground itself disappears.

This ground. The one right here.

I look down. Dry. Completely dry. A puff of dust hangs where the elephant slid. People are chatting, stretching, craning to see what’s next. Not one of them is looking at the floor.

I am. There’s space under those boards. Is that where water would go? Where would it even come from?

Nobody has written Dio’s sentence yet. I’ve read it. My strip of sunlight is getting thinner, and I can’t tell whether I’ll see this sand turn into water. All I can do is wait and watch.

Or is it? If the water really is coming, what should I do now?

[CH09 | 9:05-9:40 | 调性由轻转重，确立唯一知情者与紧迫感]
Warn him. Before it starts.

People are cheering. I can’t. I don’t want this day to go on.

Tullia has crept to the foot of the stairs. “I asked around,” she whispers. “The water is today.”

I only have her word. Dio names no day for it. His day-by-day schedule belongs to another venue, outside the city.

No one around me has his account. I’m alone with it, and with the date Titus dies: next year.

Before I risk this, can I trust that account?

[CH10 | 9:40-10:55 | 把反对证据和支持理由逐一正面摆出，同时彩排要说的话]
Not completely.

I edge along the wall toward the emperor’s box, rehearsing. “Caesar, take care of your health.” Under that, I’m arguing with myself.

Dio wrote late. Another Roman writer, Suetonius, puts Titus’s mock sea battle somewhere else, in an old naval basin. Martial’s show poems mention water, but their date and occasion are uncertain.

Still, it may be possible. A 2007 study by engineer Martin Crapper argued the arena could be filled. He pointed to plaster lining underground and a possible branch from an aqueduct.

But no archaeological evidence shows how that supply got in or was controlled. Modern estimates for filling run from about half an hour to several hours. That’s an awkward fit for “suddenly.”

Some scholars doubt it, pointing to missing pipes and a small arena. Heinz-Jürgen Beste suggests specially built small boats may have been used.

Even the space under the boards is disputed. The site’s official park says it was wood at the opening. Others say it was built later.

So it could have happened. I can’t call it proven.

The sunlight is nearly gone. If I go to Titus now, I may miss what I came to see. If I wait, he gets no warning.

I go. Will anyone near him listen?

[CH11 | 10:55-11:30 | 干预被客气挡下，任务以尽力而无效收束]
An attendant steps into my path below the box.

“Please,” I say. “Tell the emperor to take care. He may not live past next year.”

He listens to every word. “Caesar thanks you for your concern,” he says gently. “This way, please.”

His hand turns me around.

I know what he won’t hear. Titus dies next September, aged 41.

The strip of sun has vanished. There’s no second try. I tried.

I should leave. Instead, I slip back to the end wall and look down.

Does that sand become water?

[CH12 | 11:30-12:30 | 按进程呈现场面发生，旁观者的轻松反衬知情者的沉重，回收沙地埋点]
It does, in this journey.

First the sand darkens along the edge. Then it shines. Puddles find each other. Footprints soften and vanish. The ground I came to see slides out of sight. Remember your guess?

Boats lift and begin to move. Two sides close in, Corcyraeans against Corinthians, just as Dio tells it. Wood knocks on wood. Men shout across the water.

Martial has words for anyone arriving late: don’t let this water and these boats fool you. A moment ago, this was land.

When the boats are gone, I see killing.

I want to turn away. I make myself look.

Dio puts the animal dead at about 9,000, tame and wild. His count covers the celebrations for both this theatre and the new baths. Some women of low standing helped kill them. My face is wet.

Everyone pictures the Colosseum as a sandy arena. What a Roman historian wrote about its opening in 80 AD is something else entirely.

I’m 26, and I’ve come here from the present day. In Rome, I’m a nobody, a woman from outside. I’m in a dark cloak, way up at the back. Everything I know about this place is from films. I’m here to check what the opening actually looked like.

My seat is free. The front is for senators. Obviously, I am going to try to get to the front row anyway. I want that ground up close. Here we go.

[PENDING PRODUCER CONFIRMATION] I used Roman writings and standing ruins to rebuild this world. Where historians argue, I’ll tell you. My time travel, sneaking and conversations are invented.

Just between you and me: senators’ seats, the emperor’s box, the sand. I want to get close. I also want to warn Emperor Titus. He dies next year. First, can I even get in? Wish me luck.

[CH02 | 1:00-1:55 | 用入场关卡让阶层制度第一次显形，并给一个意料之外的视觉细节]
Luck holds. I can get in. My stomach just doesn’t believe it yet.

I’m in line, hood low, praying nobody asks me anything. In my hand is a token with my section, row and seat, or so the usual story goes. And the price? Nothing. Entry is free.

Then comes the catch. Free doesn’t mean sit wherever you like. Your place in society picks your seat. I look like a nobody, so I’m going up.

Wait. Look at that.

A number, cut into the stone and painted red. It jumps right out. The crowd pours in through 76 numbered arches, each one swallowing its own stream of people. In my own time, you can still read 29 of those numbers on the north side. Today the paint is bright.

I step through and look up. Oh. People everywhere, stacked row over row into the sky. A common estimate says this place holds about 50,000.

And I’m headed for the very top. What’s it actually like up there?

[CH03 | 1:55-2:55 | 用身体感受建立真实感，用现代参照制造幽默，考据不确定处点明]
Tight. That’s the first thing.

My legs are done with stairs. I squeeze in sideways, with one shoulder on my left and one elbow on my right. Somebody’s knees are in my back. I lean forward to find the field. There it is. Tiny.

You know the last row of a stadium, where you just watch the big screen? This is that row. No screen. I can see shapes moving on a pale oval, and that’s about it. I could have learned more from a postcard.

There’s a rule behind this. If the old one from Augustus, an earlier emperor, still holds here, I fail it twice: I’m a woman, and my cloak is dark.

The woman beside me shifts to make room, and looks me over while she does it. Who exactly am I squeezed in with?

[CH04 | 2:55-4:05 | 把普通观众人化，给食物考据细节，并预告即将发生的集体活动]
“First time here?” she asks.

Her name is Tullia. She sells lamp wicks from a stall with no roof, and when it rains, her whole stock is ruined. She has shut up shop for the day, and she is not going home empty-handed. Her words.

“One silver piece of tableware,” she says, “and I rent a place with a roof.”

“And you’re from where?”

“North,” I say. “Very north.”

My accent is strange. I’m sitting too stiffly. She notices both.

Luckily, strange has company up here. The poet Martial praised these shows by listing who came to watch: people from Thrace and Sarmatia, from Arabia and Ethiopia. Maybe I’m just one more foreigner.

Tullia offers me a fig. All around us, people are unwrapping food and settling in. I’m reaching for a second one when she catches my wrist.

“Keep your hands empty,” she says.

She nods across the bowl of the building. There’s the emperor’s box, and in it a small figure getting to his feet. That’s Titus. The whole top level seems to lean forward at once.

“He’s going to throw the balls.”

What happens to these seats when those little balls come down?

[CH05 | 4:05-5:20 | 集体高光，收束上一章活动悬念，配角起疑并发出私下谈话邀约]
They explode.

A little wooden ball drops from on high, and our whole row lunges for it. I jump. I miss. I get an elbow, a stomped toe and a face full of somebody’s sleeve. We came from all over, and now we’re all making the same greedy face. I can’t stop laughing.

Cassius Dio, a Roman historian writing more than a century later, says each ball carried writing. Catch one and you trade it in for food, clothing, gold or silver vessels, horses, cattle.

And slaves.

I stop laughing. That’s a person. One of these little things, bouncing off people’s fingers, can hand a human being to a stranger. People are still grabbing. My arms stay down.

Then something hard hits my palm. Tullia has scooped up a ball and closed my fingers around it.

“You looked like you needed help,” she says. “Open it. What does it say?”

I twist it in my hand and show her the writing. Her lips move. Then they stop.

“A silver vessel,” she whispers. Her roof. Right there, in my hand.

She looks from the ball to me, and this time she really looks. “You can’t read it, can you? You catch like you’ve never had hands. And that’s no northern accent.” Her voice drops. “Behind that post. Now.”

What will it cost to keep her quiet?

[CH06 | 5:20-6:40 | 向配角坦白身份换取路线情报，限时伪装完成层级突破]
One wooden ball. And I think I can get more than silence for it.

We’re squeezed behind the post. “I won’t tell you where I’m from,” I say. “But this is yours if you can get me down to that sand.”

Tullia doesn’t touch it yet. She counts my problems on her fingers. “Dark cloak. Woman. And the front belongs to senators. Nobody can get you a seat down there.”

My heart sinks.

“But messengers don’t sit,” she says.

A narrow passage runs along the edge, behind the front seats. People carrying word for important men use it. They keep moving, they keep their heads down, and they stop only in the shadows by the end wall.

She pulls off her pale wrap. “This covers your cloak. You’re someone’s servant with a message. That’s all you are.”

Then she points down the side stairs. A doorkeeper guards the opening into the passage. Right now he’s stepping away to eat.

“See that strip of sunlight on the wall? When it’s gone, he’s back. If you’re still on the far side, you don’t come out this way.” She plucks the ball from my fingers. “I’ll wait at the stairs. I want that wrap back.”

So down I go, in a borrowed wrap, heading where I have no right to be. The doorway is empty. I slip through. A man coming the other way glances at me, and my mouth goes dry. “Message,” I say, and point ahead like it’s urgent. He flattens himself against the wall and lets me by.

I don’t sit. I don’t dare. But I’m standing by the end wall, level with the senators, right next to the field.

How different is it down here?

[CH07 | 6:40-7:55 | 禁区奇观与阶层硬对照，中点观众自测，埋下脚下这层地面的疑问]
Completely. Oh my god. Look at the room they have.

Upstairs I had knees in my back. Down here a man can spread his arms. I tuck myself into the shadow and try to look like furniture.

And there’s Titus. From the top, he was a speck. Now he’s a man, leaning on one elbow, turning to catch something an attendant says. He rubs the back of his neck. He looks like someone with a very long day ahead.

Then the field. It was tiny from the top. Now it’s everything.

Cranes are fighting, all wings and legs. Then elephants, four of them, going at each other so close that I feel it in my knees. The man nearest me is picking his teeth.

One elephant skids, and the sand scrapes away. Wood. The floor is planks with sand spread on top, and there’s a hollow space underneath. The site’s official archaeological park says that space was fitted out in timber at the opening, so that’s the floor I’m picturing.

Take a guess with me. With sand, boards and empty space below, could this floor turn into something else?

How much wilder can this festival get?

[CH08 | 7:55-9:05 | 用本题史料推翻对场地的既有认知，并挂起是否亲眼见到的倒计时悬念]
A lot wilder. This party runs for 100 days.

And I know about one moment in it. If you’ve seen the film Gladiator II, you’ve watched ships fight inside this building, with sharks thrown in. I filed that under Hollywood. Sharks, sure. Water, sure. Why not a dragon?

Then I read Cassius Dio.

He wrote that Titus suddenly filled this very theatre with water. He brought in horses, bulls and other tame animals that had been trained to move around in it. Then came people on ships, fighting a sea battle.

No sharks. But the water is right there on the page.

This ground. The one in front of me.

I look down. Dry. Completely dry. A puff of dust still hangs where the elephant slid. People are chatting, stretching, craning to see what’s next. Not one of them is looking at the floor.

I am. I stare at the line where the sand meets the wall, hunting for a dark patch, a trickle, anything. Nothing. I can’t tell whether I’ll see it happen, today or at all.

And my strip of sunlight is already thinner. I came down here with a second job, so can I still do it in time?

[CH09 | 9:05-9:40 | 调性由轻转重，确立唯一知情者与紧迫感]
It has to be now. This is the closest I will ever stand to anyone around the emperor. Once that doorkeeper is back, my free run is over.

Then something changes on the field. The animals are being driven off. The gates at one end swing wide, and in the dark behind them I make out a high, curved shape. Is that the front of a boat?

My feet won’t move. If I stay here, I have the best view in the building of whatever comes next.

Around me, people cheer. Titus laughs at something. He has no idea what I know about next year.

I peel myself off the wall and start walking. But what if the water I’m giving up was never going to come?

[CH10 | 9:40-10:55 | 把反对证据和支持理由逐一正面摆出，同时彩排要说的话]
It might not. I edge along the passage, arguing with myself.

First, Dio wrote late, more than a century after this day. And out of 100 days of festival, he never says which one got the water. I duck behind a man carrying a tray.

Second, another Roman writer, Suetonius, puts Titus’s mock sea battle somewhere else, in an old basin built for naval shows. “Caesar,” I rehearse under my breath, “take care of your health.” Too vague. I try again.

Third, could the building even do it? An engineer, Martin Crapper, argued in 2007 that it could, with water possibly branching off an aqueduct. But no archaeological evidence shows how that water got in or was controlled. Some scholars doubt the whole thing.

Those boards with the hollow space under them? Even they’re part of the fight. The park says timber came first, and brick arrived under a later emperor, Domitian. Others say nothing was built down there until his reign.

So it could have happened. I can’t call it proven.

The box is right above me now. The sunlight on the wall is down to a sliver. “Caesar,” I whisper, one last time, “please be careful.”

Will anyone near him listen?

[CH11 | 10:55-11:30 | 干预被客气挡下，任务以尽力而无效收束]
An attendant steps into my path below the box.

“Please,” I say. “Tell the emperor to take care of himself. He may not live past next year.”

Above us, Titus is still talking, close enough that I can see his mouth move. He never looks down.

The attendant listens to every word. “Caesar thanks you for your concern,” he says gently. “This way, please.”

His hand turns me around. I try once more over my shoulder, but the crowd roars and swallows it. He walks me back along the passage and leaves me there.

The strip of sun is gone. The doorkeeper is back, filling the doorway. Behind him stands Tullia, waiting for her wrap. He looks at me and doesn’t move an inch. No way out, and no way back to the box.

I tried. All that’s left is the end wall and the field.

So does that sand become water?

[CH12 | 11:30-12:30 | 按进程呈现场面发生，旁观者的轻松反衬知情者的沉重，回收沙地埋点]
It does, in this journey.

Those boards and the hollow space under them are about to matter. First the sand darkens along the edge. Then it shines. Puddles find each other. A line of hoofprints softens, fills and vanishes. The noise of the crowd drops, then comes back twice as loud. The ground I came to see slides out of sight. Remember your guess?

Then the animals come in. Horses wade out with their heads high, snorting at the splashes. Bulls follow, shoulders pushing the water into little waves. They’ve been trained for this, and they move through it as if someone had simply flooded their field.

And then the ships. The shape behind the gate was a bow. It noses out into the light, and more follow, oars dipping. Men crowd the decks. One side plays the Corcyraeans, the other the Corinthians, two Greek peoples fighting all over again, here in the middle of Rome.

They close in. Oars clatter against oars. Wood knocks on wood. A man leaps across the gap, nearly misses, and gets hauled up by his belt. Spray reaches the front seats, and a senator wipes his face, delighted.

Martial has words for anyone arriving late: don’t let the water and the boats fool you. A moment ago, this was land.

Filling it for real would have taken from about half an hour to several hours, and even the occasion of Martial’s poem is uncertain, but here I am, watching the floor of the Colosseum ripple.

“See?” Tullia calls past the doorkeeper. “Good show.”

A hundred days of this. What does it cost, and how does it end?

[CH13 | 12:30-13:15 | 呈现庆典的代价与见证者决堤，以无解的情绪事件留余韵]
When the boats are gone, I see killing.

One crane keeps trying to stand. One wing drags in the sand. It gets halfway up, folds, and tries again. I can’t look at anything else.

Dio puts the animal dead at about 9,000, tame and wild. That’s his total for this theatre and the new public baths together. Some women of low standing helped with the killing.

Behind the doorkeeper, Tullia has a fig halfway to her mouth. She’s watching the crane too. Slowly, she lowers her hand. This time she doesn’t call it a good show.

Then come two gladiators, the pair she was waiting for, Priscus and Verus. In Martial’s poem, neither can beat the other. Titus gives them both the wooden sword that releases a fighter. Two men go in, and two men walk out. Tullia is shouting herself hoarse, and so am I.

My journey jumps to the last of the hundred days. Titus is crying, openly, in front of his people. The old writers leave no settled reason. In September of the next year, at 41, he’ll be dead.

So did I get my answer? Was it only sand and gladiators?

[CH14 | 13:15-14:00 | 回答标题，给出主题对照判断，用建筑现状回扣开头]
No. On the page, at least, the opening was more than sand and gladiators.

Back in my own time, I’m looking down at a maze of bare brick. This isn’t what lay under the floor in AD 80. I miss the noise. I miss the smell of wet sand. And somewhere in my head, Tullia still wants her wrap back.

Everyone pictures the Colosseum as a sandy arena. I did too. So the next time you see that sand in a photo or a film, remember that someone once wrote of it filled with water.

Recognizing a building and checking it are two different things.
